source_refs.note: Practice short questions written from Chapter 2 (PDF 22-53, printed 19-50); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 2 (Force and Motion), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 Define scalars and give two examples.
blocks.explanation: Scalars are physical quantities described solely by a magnitude (size or amount) without any mention of direction; a single number with its unit describes them fully. Examples: mass (2 kg), time (20 s).

book_ref.quote: Scalars are physical quantities that are described solely by a magnitude

blocks.prompt: 2 Is energy a scalar or a vector quantity? Give a reason.
blocks.explanation: Energy, the capacity to do work, is a scalar. It is fully described by a number and its unit (e.g. 25 J); no direction is needed.

book_ref.quote: Thus, scalars are directionless

blocks.prompt: 3 What are vectors? Give two examples with their values.
blocks.explanation: Vectors are physical quantities that need magnitude as well as direction for their complete specification. Examples: velocity 50 km h⁻¹ towards west; force 20 N to the right.

book_ref.quote: Those physical quantities which have magnitude well as direction for their complete specification.

blocks.prompt: 4 Differentiate between scalar and vector quantities.
blocks.explanation: Scalars need only magnitude; vectors need magnitude and direction.

book_ref.quote: Many problems in physics require to distinguish between scalar and vector quantities

rows: Need magnitude as well as direction.
Fully given by a number and its unit.
Need a number, a unit and a direction.
Examples: mass, distance, speed, time, energy, temperature.

blocks.prompt: 5 Differentiate between distance and displacement.
blocks.explanation: Distance is the total path length; displacement is the change in position with direction.

book_ref.quote: It has length, a distance (magnitude) and a direction

rows: Total length of path travelled, irrespective of direction.
Change in position of an object.

blocks.prompt: 6 Differentiate between speed and velocity.
blocks.explanation: Speed is a scalar; velocity is speed in a particular direction.

book_ref.quote: Velocity: The speed of an object in a particular direction

rows: Rate at which an object covers distance.
Speed of an object in a particular direction.

blocks.prompt: 7 How is a vector represented graphically and symbolically?
blocks.explanation: Graphically by an arrow: its length shows the magnitude and its head shows the direction. Symbolically by a bold face letter (V, F) or an arrow head over the symbol (A⃗).

book_ref.quote: A good way to represent a vector quantity is to use a vector diagram

blocks.prompt: 8 What are rectangular components of a vector?
blocks.explanation: A component is the effective value of a vector in a given direction. Components along mutually perpendicular directions (at right angles to each other) are called rectangular components, e.g. Ax and Ay with A = Ax + Ay.

book_ref.quote: It is usually convenient to resolve a vector into its components along the mutually perpendicular directions.

blocks.prompt: 9 A velocity of 40 m s⁻¹ is directed at 60° to the x-axis. Find its rectangular components.
blocks.explanation:
vx = v cos θ = 40 × cos 60° = 20 m s⁻¹
vy = v sin θ = 40 × sin 60° = 40 × 0.866 = 34.6 m s⁻¹

book_ref.quote: Let there be a vector A⃗ represented by a line OP making an angle θ with the x-axis.

blocks.prompt: 10 The rectangular components of a force are Fx = 5 N and Fy = 12 N. Find the magnitude and direction of the force.
blocks.explanation:
F = √(Fx² + Fy²) = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13 N
θ = tan⁻¹(Fy/Fx) = tan⁻¹(12/5) = 67.4° with the x-axis

book_ref.quote: If the rectangular components of a vector as shown in Fig.(2.1) are given

blocks.prompt: 11 Two forces of equal magnitude F act on a body. Their resultant has magnitude √2 F. Find the angle between them.
blocks.explanation:
Taking F₁ along x: Rx = F + F cos θ, Ry = F sin θ.
R² = (F + F cos θ)² + (F sin θ)² = 2F² + 2F² cos θ.
2F² = 2F² + 2F² cos θ, so cos θ = 0 and θ = 90°.

book_ref.quote: x-component of their resultant will be

blocks.prompt: 12 Differentiate between the scalar product and the vector product of two vectors.
blocks.explanation: The scalar product gives a scalar; the vector product gives a vector.

book_ref.quote: There are two types of vector multiplications.

rows: A × B = AB sin θ n̂
Result is a vector, perpendicular to the plane of A and B.
Examples: torque τ = r × F; F = q(v × B)

blocks.prompt: 13 Give the physical interpretation of the scalar product A.B.
blocks.explanation: Bring A and B to a common origin. Then A.B = A × (projection of B on A) = A(B cos θ). Similarly B.A = B(A cos θ). So A.B is the magnitude of one vector times the component of the other in its direction.

book_ref.quote: For physical interpretation of dot product of two vectors

blocks.prompt: 14 A force of 40 N moves a body 5 m in a direction at 60° to the force. Find the work done.
blocks.explanation: Work = F.d = Fd cos θ = 40 N × 5 m × cos 60° = 200 × 0.5 = 100 J

book_ref.quote: whose point of application moves a distance d in a direction making an angle θ

blocks.prompt: 15 Show that the scalar product is commutative.
blocks.explanation: A.B = AB cos θ and B.A = BA cos θ = AB cos θ. Hence A.B = B.A: the order of multiplication does not matter, so the scalar product is commutative.

book_ref.quote: In other words, scalar product is commutative.

blocks.prompt: 16 What is the scalar product of (i) two parallel vectors (ii) two antiparallel vectors (iii) a vector with itself?
blocks.explanation:
(i) θ = 0°: A.B = AB cos 0° = AB
(ii) θ = 180°: A.B = AB cos 180° = -AB
(iii) A.A = AA cos 0° = A²

book_ref.quote: Thus for parallel vectors (θ = 0°)

blocks.prompt: 17 Two vectors have components Ax = 2, Ay = 2, Az = 1 and Bx = 2, By = 1, Bz = 2. Find the angle between them.

book_ref.quote: Equation (2.6) can be used to find the angle between two vectors.

blocks.prompt: 18 Why is A × B = -B × A?
blocks.explanation: By the right hand rule, rotating A into B gives the thumb in one direction; rotating B into A reverses the sense of rotation, so the thumb points the opposite way. The magnitudes are equal (AB sin θ), so B × A is opposite in sign to A × B.

book_ref.quote: Because of this direction rule

blocks.prompt: 19 Show that the cross product of two parallel vectors is a null vector.
blocks.explanation: For parallel vectors θ = 0° or 180°, and sin 0° = sin 180° = 0. So A × B = AB sin θ n̂ = 0, a null vector. As a result A × A = 0.

book_ref.quote: because for such vectors θ = 0° or 180°

blocks.prompt: 20 Two adjacent sides of a rectangle are represented by vectors of 6 cm and 4 cm. Use the vector product to find its area.
blocks.explanation: Area = |A × B| = AB sin θ = 6 cm × 4 cm × sin 90° = 24 cm²

book_ref.quote: The magnitude of A⃗ x B⃗ is equal to the area of the parallelogram

blocks.prompt: 21 Give two examples of the vector product from physics.
blocks.explanation:
(i) Torque: the turning effect of a force F applied at position vector r, τ = r × F.
(ii) Magnetic force on a charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B, F = q(v × B).

book_ref.quote: The force F⃗ on a particle of charge q and velocity v⃗

blocks.prompt: 22 For two vectors, |A × B| = 5 units and A.B = 5√3 units. Find the angle between them.
blocks.explanation: AB sin θ / AB cos θ = 5/(5√3), so tan θ = 1/√3 and θ = 30°.

book_ref.quote: Rotate the First vector A⃗ into B⃗

blocks.prompt: 23 What are the equations of motion? Under what condition can they be applied?
blocks.explanation: They describe motion in terms of velocity, position and time: vf = vi + at (velocity-time), S = vit + ½at² (position-time), 2aS = vf² - vi² (velocity-position). They apply only to objects moving in a straight line with constant acceleration.

book_ref.quote: There are three ways to pair these variables up

blocks.prompt: 24 What do the slope and the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
blocks.explanation:
Slope of the velocity-time line = acceleration (a = BC/AC).
Area under the graph = displacement (distance) covered, e.g. S = area OABD.

book_ref.quote: First equation of motion can be derived using velocity time graph

blocks.prompt: 25 A train moving at 15 m s⁻¹ accelerates uniformly at 0.5 m s⁻² for 30 s. Find its final velocity.

book_ref.quote: Suppose a body is moving with uniform acceleration along a straight line

blocks.prompt: 26 A body starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 3 m s⁻² for 6 s. How far does it travel?
blocks.explanation: S = vit + ½at² = 0 + ½ × 3 × 6² = ½ × 3 × 36 = 54 m

book_ref.quote: using the definition of velocity as rate of change of displacement

blocks.prompt: 27 Why is average velocity used in deriving the second equation of motion?
blocks.explanation: Displacement = velocity × time holds when velocity is constant. In accelerated motion the velocity is not constant, so the average velocity (vi + vf)/2 is used: S = (vi + vf)/2 × t.

book_ref.quote: we can use average velocity instead of velocity

blocks.prompt: 28 A car slows uniformly from 30 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹ over a distance of 100 m. Find its acceleration.
blocks.explanation:
2aS = vf² - vi²
a = (10² - 30²)/(2 × 100) = (100 - 900)/200 = -4 m s⁻²
The negative sign shows retardation.

book_ref.quote: Let the displacement of the body be S during this time interval.

blocks.prompt: 29 What sign convention is used with the equations of motion for straight-line motion?
blocks.explanation: If the direction of motion does not change, vector quantities are handled like scalars. The initial velocity is taken as positive, and a negative sign is given to any quantity whose direction is opposite to the initial velocity (e.g. retardation).

book_ref.quote: If its direction of motion does not change, then all the vector quantities can be manipulated like scalars.

blocks.prompt: 30 A car moving at 54 km h⁻¹ is stopped uniformly in 3 s. Find its acceleration.
blocks.explanation:
vi = 54 × 1000/3600 = 15 m s⁻¹, vf = 0
a = (vf - vi)/t = (0 - 15)/3 = -5 m s⁻² (retardation)

book_ref.quote: Final velocity = vf = 300 km h⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 31 What is meant by free fall? What did Galileo state about it?
blocks.explanation: A body falling under the action of gravity alone falls freely with uniform acceleration g = 9.8 m s⁻². According to Galileo, all bodies fall freely in vacuum with the same acceleration g, so bodies dropped from the same height strike the ground with the same velocity.

book_ref.quote: all bodies fall freely (in vacuum) under the acceleration due to gravity

blocks.prompt: 32 Write the equations of motion for a freely falling body and state the sign convention for g.
blocks.explanation:
Putting a = g: vf = vi + gt; h = vit + ½gt²; vf² - vi² = 2gh.
g is taken positive for a falling body (vi = 0) and negative for a body projected vertically upward.

book_ref.quote: it is taken positive for a falling body (when initial velocity is zero)

blocks.prompt: 33 A stone is dropped from a height of 44.1 m. Find the time to reach the ground and its velocity on striking the ground.

book_ref.quote: A body falling freely under the action of gravity is the most familiar example

blocks.prompt: 34 A ball is thrown vertically upward with a velocity of 14.7 m s⁻¹. Find the maximum height reached and the time taken to reach it.

book_ref.quote: The equations of motion for a freely falling body, on putting a = g, become

blocks.prompt: 35 What is a projectile? Give two examples.
blocks.explanation: A body projected at some angle with the horizontal (or horizontally from a height) that moves under gravity alone is a projectile; its motion is two dimensional motion under constant acceleration due to gravity. Examples: a football kicked by a player; a missile fired from a launching pad.

book_ref.quote: all projected at some angles with the horizontal, are called projectiles

blocks.prompt: 36 Why does the horizontal velocity of a projectile remain constant?
blocks.explanation: Ignoring air friction, the only force on the projectile is gravity, which acts vertically. No horizontal force acts, so by Newton's first law ax = 0 and vfx = vix = vi cos θ throughout the flight.

book_ref.quote: So its horizontal velocity will remain unchanged

blocks.prompt: 37 One ball is dropped and another is projected horizontally from the same height at the same instant. Which reaches the ground first? Why?
blocks.explanation: Both reach together. The vertical motion of each starts with zero vertical velocity and has acceleration g; the horizontal velocity does not affect the vertical motion. Their vertical displacements are equal at every instant.

book_ref.quote: A photograph of two balls released simultaneously

blocks.prompt: 38 Write the expressions for the magnitude and direction of the velocity of a projectile at any instant.
blocks.explanation:
vfx = vi cos θ; vfy = vi sin θ - gt
Magnitude: v = √(vfx² + vfy²)
Direction with horizontal: tan φ = vfy/vfx

book_ref.quote: Now we consider the vertical motion.

blocks.prompt: 39 Define time of flight and write its expression for a projectile fired from the ground.
blocks.explanation: Time of flight is the time taken by the body from the place of projection to the place where it hits the ground. Putting S = 0 (same level) in the vertical motion: t = 2vi sin θ / g.

book_ref.quote: because body goes up and comes back to the same level

blocks.prompt: 40 A ball is projected from the ground at 49 m s⁻¹ at 30° to the horizontal. Find its time of flight.

book_ref.quote: If the body is projecting with velocity vi making angle θ with the horizontal

blocks.prompt: 41 A projectile is fired at 20 m s⁻¹ at 60° to the horizontal. Find the maximum height reached.

book_ref.quote: because the body comes to rest after reaching the highest point

blocks.prompt: 42 What is the effect of air resistance on the height of a projectile?
blocks.explanation: Air resistance decreases the upward velocity of the projectile, so the maximum height it attains is reduced.

book_ref.quote: the upward velocity of the projectile will decrease and hence its height will also decrease

blocks.prompt: 43 Define the range of a projectile and write its expression.
blocks.explanation: Range is the maximum distance covered by a projectile in the horizontal direction. R = vix × t = (vi cos θ)(2vi sin θ/g) = (vi²/g) sin 2θ.

book_ref.quote: To determine the range R of the projectile

blocks.prompt: 44 A stone is projected at 30 m s⁻¹ at 15° to the horizontal from level ground. Find its range.

book_ref.quote: Range R = (vi²/g) sin2θ = (vi²/g) sin60°

blocks.prompt: 45 How do the height and range of a projectile change when the angle of projection is less than or more than 45° (same speed)?
blocks.explanation:
Less than 45°: both the height reached and the range are less.
More than 45°: the height attained is more, but the range is again less.
The range is maximum at 45°.

book_ref.quote: When the angle of projectile is larger than 45°

blocks.prompt: 46 Why is the path of a high-speed projectile in air not a perfect parabola?
blocks.explanation: Air resistance is not constant during the flight; it decreases as the object slows down. So the trajectory is skewed, with a steeper descent than ascent, and falls short of the parabolic path.

book_ref.quote: In the presence of air friction the trajectory of a high speed projectile falls short of a parabolic path.

blocks.prompt: 47 A ball is thrown horizontally at 10 m s⁻¹ from a height of 4.9 m. Find how far from the base it lands.
blocks.explanation:
Vertical: y = ½gt², t = √(2 × 4.9/9.8) = 1 s
Horizontal: x = vx t = 10 × 1 = 10 m

book_ref.quote: Hence horizontal distance x is given by

blocks.prompt: 48 Define linear momentum. Is it a scalar or a vector? Give its SI unit.
blocks.explanation: Linear momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = mv (Newton's 'quantity of motion'). It is a vector with the direction of velocity. SI unit: kg m s⁻¹, also written N s.

book_ref.quote: The faster the object is travelling, the harder is to stop it.

blocks.prompt: 49 Show that N s is the same unit as kg m s⁻¹.
blocks.explanation:
1 N = 1 kg m s⁻² (from F = ma).
So 1 N s = 1 kg m s⁻² × s = 1 kg m s⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: if two objects move with the same velocity, then it is more difficult to stop the massive of the two

blocks.prompt: 50 Why is the momentum form of Newton's second law more general than F = ma?
blocks.explanation: F = (mvf - mvi)/t can also be used when the mass of the body changes while it accelerates, e.g. a rocket that loses mass as its fuel is burnt and ejected. F = ma assumes constant mass.

book_ref.quote: because it can easily be extended to account for changes as the body accelerates

blocks.prompt: 51 A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at 15 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 10 m s⁻¹. Find the impulse on the ball.
blocks.explanation:
Take the initial direction positive: vi = +15 m s⁻¹, vf = -10 m s⁻¹.
Impulse = mvf - mvi = 0.2 × (-10 - 15) = -5 N s (directed away from the wall).

book_ref.quote: when a bat hits a cricket ball, the force certainly varies from instant to instant

blocks.prompt: 52 Kicking a stone hurts more than kicking a football. Why?
blocks.explanation: F = (mvf - mvi)/t. The stone stops the foot in about 1/100 s, the football in about 1/10 s. For a similar change in momentum, the shorter time with the stone gives a much larger force on the foot.

book_ref.quote: (a) Stone, 1/100 second (b) Football, 1/10 second.

blocks.prompt: 53 Does a moving object have impulse? Explain.
blocks.explanation: No. A moving object has momentum (mv). Impulse is the product of a force and the time for which it acts (F × t); it exists only when a force acts, and it equals the change in momentum.

book_ref.quote: Does a moving object have impulse?

blocks.prompt: 54 How do padded helmets and seatbelts reduce injury?
blocks.explanation: A padded helmet extends the time of a collision, so for the same change in momentum the force (F = Δp/t) on the head is smaller. Seatbelts prevent passengers from moving forward when a car stops quickly, so the chance of injury is greatly reduced.

book_ref.quote: Thus, the chance of injury is greatly reduced.

blocks.prompt: 55 What is an isolated system? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: A system on which no external agency exerts any force. Example: molecules of a gas enclosed in a glass vessel at constant temperature; they collide with one another but no external agency exerts a force on them.

book_ref.quote: the molecules of a gas enclosed in a glass vessel at constant temperature constitute an isolated system

blocks.prompt: 56 Why is the total change in momentum of an isolated two-ball system zero during a collision?
blocks.explanation: The forces between the balls are action and reaction: F′ = -F, so F + F′ = 0. Then (F + F′)t = Δp₁ + Δp₂ = 0, i.e. m1v1 + m2v2 = m1v1′ + m2v2′.

book_ref.quote: Consequently, the total change in momentum of the isolated two ball system is zero.

blocks.prompt: 57 A 5 kg ball at 2 m s⁻¹ and a 3 kg ball at 4 m s⁻¹ move towards each other and collide. The 5 kg ball rebounds at 1 m s⁻¹. Find the velocity of the 3 kg ball.
blocks.explanation:
Take the 5 kg ball's direction positive.
Before: 5 × 2 + 3 × (-4) = -2 kg m s⁻¹
After: 5 × (-1) + 3v = -2, so 3v = 3 and v = 1 m s⁻¹ (in the 5 kg ball's original direction).

book_ref.quote: As both the balls are moving towards one another, so their velocities are of opposite sign.

blocks.prompt: 58 Which quantities are conserved in all collisions, and which only in elastic collisions?
blocks.explanation: Momentum and total energy are conserved in all types of collisions. Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions; in an inelastic collision part of it changes into other forms.

book_ref.quote: It is to be noted that momentum and total energy are conserved in all types of collisions.

blocks.prompt: 59 Why do two colliding tennis balls rebound with smaller velocities?
blocks.explanation: Part of the K.E. is lost, partly due to friction as the molecules in the balls move past one another when the balls distort, and partly due to its change into heat and sound. The collision is inelastic.

book_ref.quote: When two tennis balls collide then, after collision

blocks.prompt: 60 In a one-dimensional elastic collision, what is the relation between the relative velocities before and after the collision?
blocks.explanation: (v1 - v2) = -(v1′ - v2′). The relative velocity has the same magnitude before and after but is reversed: the relative velocity of approach equals the relative velocity of separation in magnitude.

book_ref.quote: is the velocity of first ball relative to the second ball

blocks.prompt: 61 How does a squash player make use of an elastic collision?
blocks.explanation: The light ball (m1) hits the massive wall (m2 >> m1) at rest. Then v1′ = -v1 and v2′ = 0: the ball bounces back with the same speed while the wall stays at rest.

book_ref.quote: This means that m₁ will bounce back with the same velocity while m₂ will remain stationary.

blocks.prompt: 62 What happens when a massive body collides elastically with a light body at rest?
blocks.explanation: With m1 >> m2 and v2 = 0: v1′ ≈ v1 and v2′ ≈ 2v1. The massive body goes on with practically no change in velocity, and the light body moves forward with about twice the velocity of the incident body.

book_ref.quote: there is practically no change in the velocity of massive body

blocks.prompt: 63 A 50 g ball moving at 4 m s⁻¹ collides elastically head-on with a 150 g ball at rest. Find their velocities after the collision.

book_ref.quote: The initial velocity of the first ball is 9 m s⁻¹ to the right

blocks.prompt: 64 What is an elastic collision in two dimensions?
blocks.explanation: When bodies travelling along an axis do not travel along the same axis after the collision (a glancing, not head-on collision), it is two-dimensional. If it is elastic, the system conserves both its total linear momentum and its total kinetic energy.

book_ref.quote: the system of bodies conserves both its total linear momentum and total kinetic energy

blocks.prompt: 65 Write the momentum equations along the x- and y-axes for a 2D elastic collision in which m2 is initially at rest.
blocks.explanation:
x-axis: m1v1i = m1v1f cos θ1 + m2v2f cos θ2
y-axis: 0 = m1v1f sin θ1 - m2v2f sin θ2, i.e. m1v1f sin θ1 = m2v2f sin θ2

book_ref.quote: Momentum conservation along x-axis is:

blocks.prompt: 66 A ball dropped on a floor does not rebound to the same height. Why?
blocks.explanation: The collision with the floor is inelastic. Part of the ball's kinetic energy is changed into other forms such as sound and heat, so less K.E. is left to raise it to the same height.

book_ref.quote: it does not rebound to the same height

blocks.prompt: 67 A 2 kg ball moving at 3 m s⁻¹ strikes an identical ball at rest. After the collision the balls move at 2.4 m s⁻¹ and 1.8 m s⁻¹ in different directions. Is the collision elastic?
blocks.explanation:
K.E.i = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J
K.E.f = ½ × 2 × 2.4² + ½ × 2 × 1.8² = 5.76 + 3.24 = 9 J
K.E. is conserved, so the collision is elastic.

book_ref.quote: Prove that collision is elastic in nature.

blocks.prompt: 68 What is a perfectly inelastic collision? Write the common velocity after such a collision in one dimension.
blocks.explanation: A collision in which the bodies stick together after the collision and move as a single body. From conservation of momentum: vf = (m1v1i + m2v2i)/(m1 + m2); if the target is at rest, vf = m1v1i/(m1 + m2).

book_ref.quote: Consider two bodies having masses m₁ and m₂, moving with velocities

blocks.prompt: 69 A 1 kg body hits a 4 kg body at rest and they stick together. What fraction of the kinetic energy is lost?
blocks.explanation: Fraction lost = m2/(m1 + m2) = 4/(1 + 4) = 0.8, i.e. 80% of the initial K.E. is lost.

book_ref.quote: Let us investigate the kinetic energies of bodies colliding inelastically.

blocks.prompt: 70 A 3 kg body moving at 10 m s⁻¹ hits a 2 kg body at rest and they stick together. Find the common velocity and the K.E. lost.

book_ref.quote: It shows that velocity of m₁ is reduced by the mass ratio

blocks.prompt: 71 Why is the collision between a bat and a ball inelastic?
blocks.explanation: Some kinetic energy is lost because the ball compresses and deforms, and energy is also converted into heat and sound. The bat also absorbs some energy. So not all the initial K.E. is conserved.

book_ref.quote: In real-world collisions, a ball and bat show an inelastic behavior.

blocks.prompt: 72 In a 2D perfectly inelastic collision, how is the direction φ of the common velocity found?
blocks.explanation:
Divide the y-momentum equation (2.40) by the x-momentum equation (2.39):
φ = tan⁻¹[(m1v1i sin θ1 + m2v2i sin θ2)/(m1v1i cos θ1 + m2v2i cos θ2)]

book_ref.quote: The angle φ of the final velocity

blocks.prompt: 73 Why are the velocities not resolved into components when finding the K.E. lost in a 2D inelastic collision?
blocks.explanation: Kinetic energy is a scalar quantity, so only the magnitudes of the velocities are needed: (K.E)i = ½m1v1i² + ½m2v2i² and (K.E)f = ½Mvf².

book_ref.quote: Since K.E. is a scalar quantity

blocks.prompt: 74 Why is a car crash an inelastic collision?
blocks.explanation: The vehicles crumple, deform and absorb the impact energy, so they do not bounce back. Most of the kinetic energy is lost as heat, sound and damage to the vehicles.

book_ref.quote: This energy absorption slows down the cars, stopping them from bouncing back.

blocks.prompt: 75 How does a rocket move forward?
blocks.explanation: Burning fuel becomes high-pressure gas, expelled at very high velocity from the rear. The gas and the rocket push against each other: the rocket gains momentum equal to that of the expelled gas but in the opposite direction. As gas keeps being expelled, the rocket keeps getting faster.

book_ref.quote: The gas and rocket push against each other and move in opposite directions.

blocks.prompt: 76 Why can a rocket work at great heights where there is little or no air?
blocks.explanation: A rocket carries its own fuel and oxygen (liquid or solid hydrogen and oxygen). It does not need air for burning, so it works where very little or no air is present.

book_ref.quote: A rocket carries its own fuel in the form of a liquid or solid hydrogen and oxygen.

blocks.prompt: 77 Why is a rocket made of several rockets linked together?
blocks.explanation: More than 80% of the launch mass is fuel. With several linked rockets, each one is discarded when its job is done, leaving a lighter craft that the others carry further up at ever greater speed.

book_ref.quote: When one rocket has done its job, it is discarded

blocks.prompt: 78 A rocket of mass 4.0 × 10⁶ kg ejects 10000 kg of gas per second at 4000 m s⁻¹ relative to it. Find its acceleration from a = mv/M.

book_ref.quote: a typical rocket consumes about 10000 kg s⁻¹ of fuel
